caricature

KAIR-ih-kuh-chur -- four syllables, stress on the first syllable, KAIR. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Caricature is a comically distorted portrayal of a person's most distinctive features.

Boardwalk artists will sketch your caricature in five minutes, oversized ears and all.

Example

In history class, the students study an 1870s magazine caricature of a railroad tycoon. The man's actual gold watch chain has been drawn as thick as a ship's anchor chain, and his top hat rises taller than the locomotive behind him -- one glance tells you exactly how rich and self-satisfied the artist thought he was.

A caricature takes one specific person's real, recognizable features -- the watch chain, the hat, the smirk -- and blows them far past life size for comic and critical effect. A caricature always has a particular target; the joke lives in the gap between the real face and the inflated one.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mockery: Mockery is making fun of someone by any means at all -- words, mimicry, laughter. A caricature mocks through one specific channel: a portrayal, usually a drawing, that inflates the person's real features until they turn comic.

exaggeration: An exaggeration stretches a statement past the truth -- 'I waited forever' -- and it needs no target and no picture. A caricature is exaggeration with a face: it inflates one real person's recognizable features, almost always in a drawing, to make its comic point.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

likeness: a faithful, accurate image of someone

realism: showing things exactly as they are

Where it sits · how far the truth is bent — cartoon → caricature → distortion

cartoon vs. caricature: Cartoon sits below caricature: a cartoon says only that a drawing is humorous, and it may invent its subject entirely, while a caricature always aims at a real person and bends that person's actual features.

distortion vs. caricature: Distortion is the strongest of the three: a caricature bends real features for a laugh, but calling a portrayal a distortion accuses it of twisting the truth itself out of shape.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — caric-

root — caric-: to load, to overload (Italian caricare, from Late Latin carricare 'to load a wagon,' from carrus 'cart')

suffix — -ature

suffix — -ature: action or result of (as in signature) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Italian caricare meant 'to load,' rolling back to Latin carrus, 'cart,' and -ature names the result of an action, as in signature -- so a caricature is literally 'an overloading.' The artist piles more and more onto the subject's most distinctive features until the portrait is comically overloaded.

Root Check

Word Choice

A caricature targets one specific person or thing and inflates its real, recognizable features, usually in a drawing or description. Keep it apart from its unit-mate spoof, which humorously imitates a whole work, genre, or style -- a spoof copies the format of cooking shows; a caricature inflates the host's eyebrows. The word also stretches figuratively: a trial run so unfairly that reporters call it 'a caricature of justice' -- a distorted, unrecognizable version of the real thing.
